shrub.silhouette: low tangled shrub of tiny round leaves

growth.juvenile_note: Tiny winged nutlets blow across the snow and sprout in early summer on bare, moist peat or moss. The seedling has two minute oval cotyledons, then small, round, deeply round-toothed leaves on a thin reddish stem; it stays a tiny sprig for years, then branches low and layers into a knee-high spreading mat of wiry brown twigs with coin-sized crinkly leaves that turn red in autumn.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Betula nana (0.15-1 m, slow-growing seedlings, establishment from seed rare, layering and sprouting; 15 d stratification then germination within 14 d at 12 C); Wikipedia (low shade tolerance); growth, first seed and stem ages estimated.

fruiting.source: USDA FEIS (monoecious, wind-pollinated, self-incompatible; female catkins in flower early June; male catkins 10-25 mm, female 6-10 mm; seeds ripen in August and disperse from late summer to the next spring, blowing over snow); Wikipedia (fruiting catkins 5-15 mm); counts are catkins, estimated.

shrub.name: Alpenrose

growth.juvenile_note: Minute seedlings on moss or raw humus: two tiny cotyledons, then small glossy, dark green, leathery leaves with rusty-brown scaly undersides and rolled edges. For years it is a small, few-stemmed sprig; then it branches densely into a low, rounded evergreen bush, and stems that touch the ground root and spread it into a clonal patch.
growth.source: German Wikipedia Rostblaettrige Alpenrose (30-130 cm; stems 1-2 cm thick nearly 100 yr old; leaves live ~2 yr; flowers May-Jul, corolla to 2 cm, deep pink to red; capsules to 7 mm ripen from August; semi-shade light value; 440-2,840 m); germination and first flowering estimated

growth.juvenile_note: Seed shed in autumn lies under the snow and germinates right after snowmelt: 2 tiny round cotyledons, then oval grey-green leaves that are whitish (glaucous) underneath and hairy when young. Adds only a few cm a year, building a low, rounded, much-branched bush of stout knobbly twigs; wind-blasted plants stay low and sprawling.
growth.source: USDA Woody Plant Seed Manual Salix (S. glauca flowers Jun-Jul and disperses seed Sep-Nov; fall-shed willow seed overwinters and germinates quickly after snowmelt); Flora of N America (0.3-1.5 m, to 6 m in shelter); growth, first seed and lifespan estimated for a tundra shrub willow

fruiting.source: USDA Woody Plant Seed Manual Salix table (S. glauca: flowers June-July, seed dispersed Sept-Nov); Flora of N America (catkins 2-6 cm with the leaves, hairy capsules 5-9 mm); fruit set, crop and rot estimated

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal: tiny oval cotyledons, then a thread-thin green stem with small oval, finely toothed, bright green leaves. Seedlings are rare and grow very slowly; after a few years the plant is a low tuft of sharply angled, bright green, broom-like twigs that stay green through winter after the leaves drop, and rhizomes start sending up new shoots around it.
growth.source: USDA FEIS (Vaccinium myrtillus): 35-64% germination after cold, seedlings rare and initially very slow, seed production begins at about age 3, aerial shoots live up to about 15 yr, rhizomes 23-28 yr, understory dominant in conifer forests with few berries under a closed canopy; Wikipedia: 10-51 cm, can live up to 30 years.

fruiting.source: USDA FEIS (Vaccinium myrtillus): pink, cream or greenish-white urn to bell flowers borne singly in leaf axils, bees the main pollinators, round dark red to blue-black berries 5-8 mm ripening about 50 days after flowering; Wikipedia: blooms Apr-May, blue-black fruit up to 1 cm Jul-Sep, fruit persists on average 16.7 days. Fruit set and crop estimated.

ground.silhouette: flat evergreen mat with white eight-petal flowers

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal: two tiny round cotyledons, then small oblong leaves with rounded teeth, glossy dark green above and white-woolly beneath, like miniature oak leaves. The seedling's woody stem creeps and branches over limestone gravel, rooting as it goes, and slowly builds a flat evergreen mat that carries eight-petalled white flowers and twisting feathery seed plumes.
growth.source: Wikipedia Dryas octopetala (creamy white flowers with 8, occasionally up to 16, petals on 3-10 cm stalks; persistent feathery styles twisted, then spreading into a ball for wind dispersal; early-melting gravel and rock barrens, mostly on limestone). Mat growth, first flowering and age estimated (Elkington 1971 Biol. Flora, not read).

growth.juvenile_note: No seedling: a new patch starts from a broken-off fragment (trampled or carried by wind and reindeer) or, rarely, from spores that must meet a green alga. Each piece grows into a pale yellow-green, rounded head of dense, fine, star-like branching; heads pack side by side into a smooth cauliflower-like carpet 5-12 cm deep that takes decades to rebuild after fire or grazing.
growth.source: Wikipedia Cladonia stellaris (grows on average <5 mm per year under good conditions; key reindeer and caribou winter forage); Kytoviita & Crittenden 2007 and boreal lichen-woodland studies (slow recovery over decades after fire or grazing); lifespan estimated

ground.name: Reindeer lichen

growth.juvenile_note: No seedling: a new patch starts from a broken-off fragment (trampled or carried by wind and reindeer) or, rarely, from spores that must meet a green alga. The young thallus is a scatter of tiny grey stalks that branch in threes and fours, tips all bending one way; over decades they build a springy ash-grey mat up to ~10 cm deep, dying at the base while growing at the tips.
growth.source: Wikipedia Cladonia rangiferina (grows 3-11 mm/yr, 3.9-4.4 mm/yr in Finland; mats to ~10 cm, ~12 cm in humid, 4-6 cm in dry sites; can establish ~2 yr after fire but takes decades to recover; individual lives ~20-30 yr; faster growth in shadier forests)

repro.note: spores by wind and water; no flowers; needs a wet film to reproduce, so spread reads moisture not pollinators

ground.source: Tundra and open taiga; grey-white mats the caribou dig for in winter; grows millimetres a year. Index Fungorum.

canopy.name: Lodgepole pine

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal seedling with 3-6 cotyledons and a tuft of single primary needles, then short, twisted, paired needles. Young trees are dense, narrow cones with regular whorls. Open-grown shore pines become bushy, crooked and flat-topped; inland trees become slim, straight poles. Serotinous cones stay closed on the branches for decades.
growth.source: USDA Silvics (Lotan & Critchfield): viable seed commonly at 5-10 years; ~3.6 m at 20 years on medium sites; germination peaks in the 2 weeks after snowmelt; very intolerant of shade; shore pine small and short-lived; ages commonly 150-200+, old high-elevation trees to 400+

canopy.source: western North American mountains; 20–35 m. Dense even-aged stands after fire; cones open in heat. Kew POWO for the name; standard floras for range.

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal: about six needle-like cotyledons, then soft, bright-green single needles spiralled along the first-year shoot; tufted needles on short spur shoots follow from the second year. Young trees are slender, open, feathery cones with level branches that turn gold and drop every needle in autumn; on permafrost they often stay stunted and sparse for decades.
growth.source: USDA Woody Plant Seed Manual (Larix: L. gmelinii flowers May-Jun, cones ripen Sep, seed from 14-15 yr, good crops every 2-4 yr, 30-day germination tests, empty cones persist); Wikipedia (10-30 m; oldest 919 yr in Yakutia; permafrost; seed ripe 3-5 months after pollination). Growth on permafrost estimated.

fruiting.source: Wikipedia (upright cones 1-2.5 cm, green or red when young, brown when ripe, seed shed 3-5 months after pollination, old cones persist grey-black); USDA WPSM (young cones light to deep purple, ripen Sep, empty cones stay on the tree indefinitely). Set and crop estimated.

growth.juvenile_note: Tiny two-winged nutlets sprout in early summer on moss, bare soil or burnt ground. Seedlings have minute round cotyledons, then small, downy, coarsely toothed, rounded leaves on hairy reddish twigs. At the treeline the young tree soon sprouts extra stems from its base, becoming a crooked, multi-stemmed bush with dark reddish-brown bark that whitens and peels only on older stems.
growth.source: Wikipedia (short-lived tree; subarctic mountain birch small, contorted and shrubby); Atkinson 1992 Biological Flora of Betula pendula and B. pubescens (light-demanding pioneer, seed from young age, winged nutlets shed late summer to winter); treeline growth rates and ages estimated.

fruiting.source: General Betula pubescens silvics (Atkinson 1992): catkins open with the leaves in spring (May-Jun in the subarctic), wind-pollinated, fruiting catkins 2-3.5 cm break up on the tree from late summer through winter; counts are catkins, estimated.
